title: Care stocks: how to analyze care companies and providers
description: Care stocks: hospitals, care homes, pharmacy — the margin staircase, IFRS 16 leases and public money. Read care companies with the universe's own numbers.
author: AK1A Research Lab
body:
Care stocks are shares in companies running health and social care — hospitals, care homes, home care, disability services under Sweden's LSS act, and the pharmacy link between factory and patient. The business differs decisively from the health sector's other two families: pharmaceutical companies sell patent-protected molecules, medtech products with recurring consumption — care companies sell worked hours. The health branch of AK1A's universe holds 25 companies; the first two families have their guides — the third, the operators, is this one. Three seasoned names carry it: Fresenius with private hospitals in Germany, Attendo — the Nordics' largest care provider, around 33,000 employees in Sweden, Norway, Denmark and Finland — and Galenica with pharmaceutical distribution and pharmacies in Switzerland.

The guide walks through the mechanisms with the universe's own numbers (raw data 2026-09-03, 09-17, 09-18). As always: education in method, never advice about individual stocks.

## What are care stocks — people, not molecules

The family splits into three sub-families, three different economies. Fresenius runs hospitals reimbursed per treatment case: volume is needs-driven and ultimately paid by public coffers. Attendo runs elder care, LSS and individual and family care on municipal contracts in four countries — operations mandated by law, need growing with demographics, price set in procurement, not an open market. Galenica stands between factory and patient: distribution and pharmacy are logistics per package, low margin but very stable volume.

Common to all three: the customer ultimately sits with the taxpayer, staff is the largest cost item, the premises are rented. One number captures the family: 2025 revenue of SEK 18,991 million with 33,000 employees — roughly SEK 575,000 per employee. Scale is laid in people, not machines — the root of the difference from pharma, whose leaders earn many times more per employee.

## The margin staircase — from molecule to human

Sort the health branch's 25 gross margins and a staircase appears: Genmab 93.0 percent, Eli Lilly 83.4, Novo Nordisk 82.0 — the medtech family around 67–74 with Sonova 73.7 and CellaVision 68.7 — Getinge 48.6 — then the operators' plain: Attendo 36.9, Fresenius 25.4 and Galenica 12.5 percent. Same industry, yet more than eighty percentage points from top to bottom.

The staircase is the geography of pricing power. The patent gives the molecule a temporary monopoly, brand and design give medtech its premium — but a worked hour in home care sets no limit on copying. Note the contrast in one universe: Roche 74.2 percent gross margin against Galenica 12.5 — 61.7 percentage points between selling intellectual property and moving packages. The operator's moat sits instead in scale, staffing quality and contract length; [the anatomy of the gross margin](/kurser/v07-bruttomarginal) and [the margin staircase with operating leverage](/kurser/ln-03-marginaltrappan-och-operativ-havstavng) go deeper on the mechanism.

## The leases in the balance sheet — the IFRS 16 lesson

Nursing homes and clinics are rented, and IFRS 16 lifts the leases into the balance sheet. Attendo therefore carries a debt-to-equity ratio of a full 3.15 — property-like numbers — while interest coverage sits at 2.5 times and debt per EBITDA at 5.28. In substance it resembles a property company's balance sheet, but without appreciation: leases are a cost item, not an asset rising with the market. Reading the balance sheet is therefore two-track: [solvency and interest coverage](/kurser/st-01-soliditet-och-rantetackning) alongside [the mechanics of leasing](/kurser/km-023-leasing).

The same rule creates a strange detail in the income statement: Attendo's EBITDA margin is reported at 7.50 percent — below the EBIT margin of 10.34 — because the source measures EBITDA after lease depreciation. Cash flow differs from accounting profit too: FCF margin 14.3 percent against net margin 5.1 percent. The whole difference sits in the timing of lease payments and working capital — [the quality of the income statement](/kurser/tx-07-fran-siffra-till-kassa) and [cash flow analysis](/kurser/km-003-kassaflodesanalysen) show the craft.

Leverage has two sides too: the ROE of 18.7 percent is carried by the debt, while ROIC at 7.57 percent lands only 0.69 percentage points above the WACC of 6.88 — a narrow value-creation margin where [the ROE calculation](/blogg/hur-raknar-man-roe) and [return on invested capital](/kurser/roic-01-avkastning-pa-investerat-kapital) tell different stories about the same company, and [the dangerous levels of the debt-to-equity ratio](/blogg/skuldsattningsgrad-vilken-niva-ar-farlig) gains new meaning when leases are the driving force.

## The revenue mechanics — taxpayer money and a political price

Operator revenues are governed by regulation, not the consumer's wallet. In Sweden, the Public Procurement Act (2016:1145) exposes the contracts to competition while the Act on Systems of Choice (2008:962), in some systems, lets the user choose the provider — two mechanisms that cap the price and aim competition at quality and cost. A lost re-procurement can move a whole municipality's care revenues to a competitor on one contract date — so contract length and renewal risk weigh heavier than next year's growth. [Regulatory risk](/kurser/rk-06-regulatorisk-risk) and [the anatomy of the regulation variable](/kurser/v18-regulatoriska) map the family; in Germany Fresenius's clinics are reimbursed per treatment case, in Switzerland Galenica operates under pharmacy regulation.

The dynamics show in the Attendo series: net profit went from minus SEK 45 million in 2022 to SEK 813 million in 2025 while revenue grew 9.4 percent per year, SEK 14,496 to 18,991 million — 2023's 19.3 percent growth was carried by integration and a staffing afterwave, then profitability turned as growth levelled off; the share has since repriced by 87.4 percent over 52 weeks. Fresenius carries the same story at larger scale: when the hospital business was spun off, revenue fell from EUR 40,840 to 22,299 million — 45.4 percent — while profit turned from minus EUR 594 to plus 1,264 million. Galenica is the opposite pole: beta 0.28, dividend yield 3.06 percent on a 78.7 percent payout, three straight up years after the fall of 2022 — essential provision rather than a turnaround.

Behind it all stands a structural driver: the aging population, [demography's clock](/kurser/mk-12-demografins-klocka). Demand for care grows regardless of the business cycle — but costs grow with wage formation, [wage formation and the cost spiral](/kurser/ma-02-lonebildning-och-kostnadsspiralen), and a labor-intensive operation has no factory absorbing the blow.

## Valuing care stocks — stability is negotiated

The staircase shows up in the multiples too. P/E: Fresenius 16.26, Attendo 19.25, Galenica 25.68 — and EV/EBIT at 14.55, 17 and 24.55 respectively. Galenica's paradox is the textbook case: the highest multiple despite the lowest ROIC, 6.82 percent — distribution value carried by volume stability rather than return on capital. Attendo's forward P/E 16.05 against trailing 19.25 shows the market expecting the profitability turn to continue, and the PEG ratios 0.79, 0.97 and 1.01 [measure stretched expectations](/blogg/peg-multipeln-svagheter-2026) against every percent of growth. The cash side: FCF yield 15.0 percent and total shareholder yield 5.7 — buybacks 4.25 percent plus dividends 1.47 — while [free cash flow yield](/kurser/vm-07-free-cash-flow-yield) weighs the operation's cash against reported profit. Setting the family in context: [the health and care sector course](/kurser/km-048-halsovardsektorn) and [the sector analysis method](/kurser/se-16-sektoranalysens-metod).

## The checklist — five steps when you analyze care stocks

1. **The family first.** Hospitals, care or the pharmacy link — three economies with different reimbursement logic, never one shared multiple.
2. **The margin against the family.** Gross margins of 36.9, 25.4 or 12.5 percent mean different things; Attendo's five-year average 33.4 percent with a spread of 4.8 percentage points shows that [unit economics](/kurser/tx-06-enhetsekonomin) — per place, per hour, per package — is the operator family's unit of account.
3. **The balance sheet through IFRS 16.** A debt-to-equity ratio of 3.15 says property logic; interest coverage of 2.5 says operator logic — read both before judging the debt.
4. **Follow the cash, not just the net.** FCF from SEK 1,165 to 2,657 million in four years — 2.28 times — while net went from minus SEK 45 to 813 million: the cash caught the turn earlier than the income statement.
5. **Map the money.** Who pays — municipality, region or patient — on which contract, how often it can be renegotiated, how much of the revenue is mandated by law. In the operator family the selling proposition is never the product but the contract.

To go further, the whole craft is in [the complete guide to Swedish stock analysis](/blogg/komplett-guide-svensk-aktieanalys-2026).

_Sources: AK1A's 100-company universe (Yahoo Finance/MarketStack/StockAnalysis on S&P data, raw data 2026-09-03/17/18); [Fresenius](https://www.fresenius.com/investors); [Attendo](https://www.attendo.com); [Galenica](https://www.galenica.com); the Health and Social Care Inspectorate, IVO ([ivo.se](https://www.ivo.se)); the Public Procurement Act (2016:1145) ([riksdagen.se](https://www.riksdagen.se/sv/dokument-och-lagar/dokument/svensk-forfattningssamling/lag-20161145-om-offentlig-upphandling_sfs-2016-1145/))._

_This is educational financial analysis, not investment advice._
